label: lem:gate-properties
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:gate-properties}
The functions $\psi$ and $\phi$ defined in equation 
equation~(\ref{eq:gate-functions}) satisfy the following
properties. 
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*),leftmargin=0.65cm]
    \item The function $\psi$ satisfies $\psi(t)=0$ for all $t \le 1/2$, and 
    $\psi(t)=1$ for all $t\ge1$.
    \item The function $\psi$ satisfies
    $0\le\psi(t)\le1$, $0\le\psi'(t)\le4$, and $|\psi''(t)|\le24$ for all $t\in{\mathbb{R}}$.
    \item The function $\phi$ satisfies
    $0<\phi(t)<2$, $\phi'(t)=\operatorname{sech}^2(t)$, and    $|\phi''(t)|\le2\phi'(t)$ for all $t\in{\mathbb{R}}$.
    \item The derivative $\phi'$ is even and holds
    $\phi'(t)>2/5$ for all $t\in[-1, 1]$.
\end{enumerate}
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md:
We illustrate the derivatives of $\psi$ and $\phi$ in Figure \ref{figure:component}. Note that the derivative $\psi'(t)$ is non-zero only for $t\in(1/2, 1)$, which is useful to construct the zero-chain. 
    Additionally, the manganite of $\phi''(t)$ always can be bounded by $2\phi'(t)$, corresponding to the $(L_0, L_1)$-smoothness.
head: environment

label: lem:hard-chain-properties
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:hard-chain-properties}
The function $\bar f_T$ defined in equation~(\ref{eq:hard-zero-chain}) satisfies the following properties.
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*),leftmargin=0.65cm]
    \item 
    The optimality gap holds $\bar f_T({\bf{0}}) - \inf_{{\bf{y}}\in{\mathbb{R}}^T}\bar f_T({\bf{y}}) =2T-1$.
    \item                                     
    For all ${\bf{y}}\in{\mathbb{R}}^T$, it holds 
    $\left\| \nabla\bar f_T({\bf{y}}) \right\| \le9\sqrt T$ 
    and $\left\| \nabla^2\bar f_T({\bf{y}}) \right\| \le 58$.
    \item                                     
    For given ${\bf{y}}=[y_1,\dots,y_T]\in{\mathbb{R}}^T$, if there exists $i\in[T]$ such that $|y_i|\le1$, then $\left\| \nabla\bar f_T({\bf{y}}) \right\| \ge\frac25$.    
    \item  For all ${\bf{y}}\in{\mathbb{R}}^T$, it holds $\left\| \nabla^2 \bar f_T({\bf{y}}) \right\| \le 160\left\| \nabla\bar f_T({\bf{y}}) \right\|$.
    \item \label{item:zero-chain-progress}  For all ${\bf{y}}\in{\mathbb{R}}^T$, it holds $\operatorname{prog}_0(\nabla\bar f_T({\bf{y}}))\le\operatorname{prog}_{1/4}({\bf{y}})+1$.
\end{enumerate}
head: environment

label: remark:fT
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{remark:fT}
Lemma \ref{lem:hard-chain-properties}(d) implies that  function $\bar f_T$ is $(0, 320)$-smooth, which is essential different with the analysis for standard smooth case \citep{carmon2020lower}.
In fact, the ratio of the gradient norm to the Hessian norm in the classical hard instance for standard smooth optimization is unbounded, so that it cannot characterize the specific hardness of $(L_0, L_1)$-smoothness.
Please refer to discussion in Appendix~\ref{appendix:disscusion}.
head: environment

label: lem:global-hard-properties
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md:
Following Remark \ref{remark:fT}, inequality (\ref{eq:global-hard-curvature}) indicates function $H_{{\bf U},\mu}$ defined in
equation~(\ref{eq:global-hard-function}) is $(\mu\log(1/\mu),300)$-smooth, going beyond the hard instance for standard smooth optimization \citep{carmon2020lower}.

label: thm:nsgd
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:nsgd}
We run Algorithm \ref{alg:sn-mb-sgd} to solve problem (\ref{eq:problem}) with  $f\in{\mathcal{F}}(L_0, L_1, \Delta)$ by using stochastic first-order oracle ${\bf{g}}:{\mathbb{R}}^d\times{\mathcal{Z}}\to{\mathbb{R}}^d$ such that     
\begin{align*}
{\mathbb{E}}_Z[{\bf{g}}({\bf{x}};Z)]=\nabla f({\bf{x}})
\qquad\text{and} \qquad
{\mathbb{E}}_Z\left[\left\| {\bf{g}}({\bf{x}};Z)-\nabla f({\bf{x}}) \right\|^p\right] \leq \sigma^p
\end{align*}
for some $\sigma\geq 0$ and $p\in(1,2]$.
By taking parameters
\begin{align}\label{eq:nsgd-parameter}
\eta =\frac{\epsilon}{4(L_0+L_1\epsilon)},\quad
\gamma\in\left[0,\frac{\epsilon}{4}\right],\quad
b=\bigg\lceil
\bigg(\frac{32\sqrt2\,\sigma}{\epsilon}\bigg)^{\frac{p}{p-1}}+1
\bigg\rceil,
\quad \text{and}\quad
T=\left\lceil\frac{4\Delta}{\eta\epsilon}\right\rceil.
\end{align}
the output satisfies ${\mathbb{E}}[\left\| \nabla f(\hat{\bf{x}}) \right\|]\leq\epsilon$.

label: eq:gate-functions1
title: Proof
body_md:
Recall that the functions $\psi$ and $\phi$ are defined as
\begin{equation}
    \psi(t):=S(2t-1) \qquad \text{and}   \qquad   \phi(t):=1+\tanh(t).
    \label{eq:gate-functions1}
\end{equation}
respectively, where
\begin{equation}
    S(u)=
    \begin{cases}
        0, & u\le 0,\\
        10u^3-15u^4+6u^5, & u\in(0,1),\\
        1, & u\ge 1.
    \end{cases}
    \label{eq:gate-S1}
\end{equation}
We verify the first-order and second-order derivatives of $S$ as
\begin{align}\label{eq:S-prime}
S'(u) = \begin{cases}
30u^2(u-1)^2,  & \text{if}~u\in(0,1), \\
0, & \text{otherwise},
\end{cases}
\end{align}
and
\begin{align}\label{eq:S-second}
    S''(u) =\begin{cases}
    60u(u-1)(2u-1),  & \text{if}~u\in(0,1) \\
    0, & \text{otherwise}.
    \end{cases}
\end{align}

We now prove each statement of the lemma.

\paragraph{The proof of statement (a).} The definitions of $\psi$ and $S$ in equations (\ref{eq:gate-S1}) and (\ref{eq:S-second}) directly shows that~$\psi(t)=0$ for all $t \le 1/2$, and $\psi(t)=1$ for all $t\ge1$.


\paragraph{The proof of statement (b).}
We first consider the value of $\psi(t)$. 
By equation equation~(\ref{eq:S-prime}), we know that $S'(t)\geq 0$ on ${\mathbb{R}}$, which implies the function $S$ is non-decreasing.
Combining the facts $S(0)=0$ and $S(1)=1$, we obtain
$0\le S(u)\le1$ for all $u\in[0,1]$.
Combing the definitions $S(u)=0$ for all~$u\leq 0$ and $S(u)=1$ for all $u\geq 1$, we know that $S(u)\in[0,1]$ on ${\mathbb{R}}$.
Hence, the definition of~$\psi(t)=S(2t-1)$ implies
\begin{equation*}                   
    0\le\psi(t)\le1.
\end{equation*}

We then consider the value of $\psi'(t)$. By the chain rule, we can write 

\begin{align}\label{eq:psi-dev}
\psi'(t) = \begin{cases}
 60(2t-1)^2(2t-2)^2,       &  t\in[ 1/2,1], \\
 0 & \text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}
\end{align}
Clearly, it holds $\psi'(t)\ge0$. 
For $t\in[1/2,1]$, we let
\[
u:=2t-1\in[0,1],
\]
which leads to
\begin{align*}
\psi'(t)= 60(2t-1)^2(2t-2)^2 = 60u^2(u-1)^2 .
\end{align*}
Since for all $u\in[0,1]$, it holds 
\[
    u(u-1) = \left(u-\frac12\right)^2 - \frac14
    \in \left[-\frac14, 0\right],
\]
which implies
\[
    \psi'(t)
    \le
    60\cdot\frac1{16}
    =
    \frac{15}{4}
    <4.
\]
Recall that $\psi'(t)=0$ for all $t\in[0, 1/2]$, 
we obtain $0\le\psi'(t)\le4$ for all $t\in{\mathbb{R}}$.

We now consider the value of $\psi''(t)$. By the chain rule, we can write 
\[
    \psi''(t)=4S''(2t-1).
\]
Equation (\ref{eq:S-second}) indicates $\psi''(t)=0$ for all $t\not\in(1/2,1)$.
Hence, we focus on the case of~$t\in(1/2,1)$, that is $u=2t-1\in(0,1)$. 
We write
\begin{equation*}
    \psi''(t)=240u(1-u)(1-2u).
                                     
\end{equation*}
and define
\[
    g(u):=u(1-u)(1-2u)
    =
    u-3u^2+2u^3.
\]
Then we have
\[
    g'(u)=1-6u+6u^2,
\]
which has critical points 
\[
    u_{+} = \frac{3+\sqrt3}{6}
    \qquad\text{and}\qquad
    u_{-} = \frac{3-\sqrt3}{6}.
\]
Since it holds $g(0)=g(1)=0$, the maximum of $|g(u)|$ on $[0,1]$ is attained at one of these critical points.
We can verify
\begin{align*}
    |g(u_+)| = |g(u_-)|=\frac{\sqrt3}{18},
\end{align*}
which implies
\[
    |\psi''(t)|
    \le
    240 \cdot \frac{\sqrt3}{18}
    <24.
\]

\paragraph{The proof of statement  (c).}
The fact $\tanh t\in(-1,1)$ directly implies 
\begin{align*}
\phi(t)=1+\tanh t\in(0,2).    
\end{align*}
We can also verify
$\phi'(t)=\operatorname{sech}^2t$ and $\phi''(t) = -2\operatorname{sech}^2(t)\tanh(t)$, which implies
\begin{align*}
    |\phi''(t)|
= 2\operatorname{sech}^2(t)|\tanh(t)|
< 2\operatorname{sech}^2(t)
= 2\phi'(t).
\end{align*}

\paragraph{The proof of statement  (d).}
The statement that $\phi'$ is even can be verifies as 
\begin{equation*}                               
    \phi'(-t)=\operatorname{sech}^2(-t)=\operatorname{sech}^2(t)=\phi'(t).
\end{equation*}
It remains to show that $\phi'(t)>2/5$ for $|t|\le1$.
For all $t\geq 0$, it holds
\[
    \phi''(t) =
    -2\operatorname{sech}^2(t)\,\tanh (t)    \le0,
\]
which implies $\phi'$ is non-increasing on $[0,\infty)$.
Therefore, for all $t\in[0,1]$, it holds
\begin{equation*}
    \phi'(t) =\operatorname{sech}^2(t)
    \ge \operatorname{sech}^2(1)
    > \frac{2}{5}.
                                 
\end{equation*}
Since $\phi'(t)$ is even, we have $|\phi'(t)|>2/5$ when $|t|\leq 1$.

label: lem:gate-paired-properties
title: Lemma
head: environment

label: eq:gate-pair-derivative-zero
title: Proof
body_md:
The expression of $\psi'(\cdot)$ in equation~(\ref{eq:psi-dev}) implies
\begin{equation}
    \psi'(t)=\psi''(t)=0
    \qquad
    \text{whenever } t\leq 1/2  \text{~~or~~}  t \geq 1.
    \label{eq:gate-pair-derivative-zero}
\end{equation}
We prove this lemma by considering the following three cases.

\paragraph{The Case of $|t|\le1/2$.}
The condition $|t|\le1/2$ implies both $t$ and $-t$ are at most $1/2$.
Hence, the definitions of $\psi(\cdot)$ and $S(\cdot)$ in equations (\ref{eq:gate-functions1}) and (\ref{eq:gate-S1}) implies $\psi(t)=\psi(-t)=0$. This results
\[
    \psi(t)+\psi(-t)=0\le1.
\]
Furthermore, equation~(\ref{eq:gate-pair-derivative-zero}) indicates
$\psi'(t)=\psi'(-t)=0$ and $\psi''(t)=\psi''(-t)=0$, which imply
\[
\psi'(t)+\psi'(-t)=0\le4
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
|\psi''(t)|+|\psi''(-t)|=0\le24.
\]


\paragraph{The Case of $t>1/2$.}
The condition $t>1/2$ implies $-t<-1/2$. Hence, the definition (\ref{eq:gate-functions1})  and equation~(\ref{eq:gate-pair-derivative-zero}) implies 
\begin{align*}
\psi(-t)=\psi'(-t)=\psi''(-t)=0.     
\end{align*}
Combining with Lemma~\ref{lem:gate-properties}(b), we obtain
\[
    \psi(t)+\psi(-t)=\psi(t)\le1,~~
    \psi'(t)+\psi'(-t)=\psi'(t)\le4,~~\text{and}~~
    |\psi''(t)|+|\psi''(-t)|=|\psi''(t)|\le24.
\]
\paragraph{The Case of $t<-1/2$.}
The condition $t<-1/2$ implies $-t>1/2$. Hence, the definition  (\ref{eq:gate-functions1}) and equation~(\ref{eq:gate-pair-derivative-zero}) implies
\begin{align*}
    \psi(t)=\psi'(t)=\psi''(t)=0.
\end{align*}
Combining with Lemma~\ref{lem:gate-properties}(b), we obtain
\[
\psi(t)+\psi(-t)=\psi(-t)\le1,~\psi'(t)+\psi'(-t)=\psi'(-t)\le4,~\text{and}~
|\psi''(t)|+|\psi''(-t)|=|\psi''(-t)|\le24.
\]

Hence, equations (\ref{eq:gate-pair-value}), (\ref{eq:gate-pair-first}), and (\ref{eq:gate-pair-second}) hold for all $t\in{\mathbb{R}}$.
head: environment

label: eq:hard-zero-chain1
title: Proof
body_md:
Recall that the function $\bar f_T$ is defined as
\begin{equation}
\bar f_T({\bf{y}}) := \sum_{i=1}^{T}A_i({\bf{y}}),
~~~~\text{where}~~
A_i({\bf{y}}):=
\begin{cases}
-\phi(y_1), & \text{if}~i=1, \\[0.1cm]
\psi(-y_{i-1})\phi(-y_i)
-
\psi(y_{i-1})\phi(y_i), & \text{otherwise}.    
\end{cases}
\label{eq:hard-zero-chain1}
\end{equation}

\paragraph{The proof of statement (a).}
According to definition (\ref{eq:gate-functions1}) and Lemma~\ref{lem:gate-properties}(a), we have $\phi(0)=1$ and~$\psi(0)=0$.
Hence, definition (\ref{eq:hard-zero-chain1}) implies
\begin{equation}
    A_i({\bf{0}})=\begin{cases}
        -1, &  \text{if}~i=1, \\
        0, &  \text{otherwise}.
    \end{cases}
    \qquad\text{and}\qquad     
    \bar f_T({\bf{0}})=-1.
    \label{eq:hard-chain-origin}
\end{equation}
For all ${\bf{y}}\in{\mathbb{R}}^T$, Lemma~\ref{lem:gate-properties}(c) implies
\[
    A_1({\bf{y}})=-\phi(y_1)>-2.
\]
Moreover, for every $i\ge2$, Lemma~\ref{lem:gate-properties}(b) and (c) implies
\[
\psi(-y_{i-1})\phi(-y_i)\ge0
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
0\le\psi(y_{i-1})\phi(y_i)<2.
\]
It follows from equation~(\ref{eq:hard-zero-chain1})
that
\[
    A_i({\bf{y}})>-2
    \qquad\text{and}\qquad
    \bar f_T({\bf{y}}) = \sum_{i=1}^T A_i({\bf{y}})>-2T.
\]
Thus, it holds
\[
    \inf_{{\bf{y}}\in{\mathbb{R}}^T}\bar f_T({\bf{y}})\ge-2T.
\]
We then consider the vector
\[
    {\bf{y}}^{(r)}= r[1,\ldots,1]^\top,
    \qquad \text{where}~~r\ge1.
\]
Lemma~\ref{lem:gate-properties}(a) implies $\psi(r)=1$ and $\psi(-r)=0$.
Consequently, definition equation~(\ref{eq:hard-zero-chain1}) implies
\[
    A_i({\bf{y}}^{(r)})
    =
    -\phi(r).
\]
for all $i\in[T]$, which results
\begin{equation}
    \lim_{r\to+\infty} \bar f_T({\bf{y}}^{(r)}) = \lim_{r\to+\infty} -T\phi(r) = -2T.
    \label{eq:hard-chain-infimum}
\end{equation}
Combining equations (\ref{eq:hard-chain-origin})
and (\ref{eq:hard-chain-infimum}) yields
\begin{equation*}
    \bar f_T({\bf{0}})-\inf_{{\bf{y}}\in{\mathbb{R}}^T}\bar f_T({\bf{y}})=2T-1.
\end{equation*}

\paragraph{The proof of statement (b).}
We first establish the uniform bound on the gradient of $\bar f_T$. Taking the derivative on equation~(\ref{eq:hard-zero-chain1}) and using the evenness of $\phi'$ from Lemma~\ref{lem:gate-properties}(d), we obtain
\small\begin{equation}\label{eq:hard-chain-gradient-coordinate}
\begin{split}    
\frac{\partial\bar f_T({\bf{y}})}{\partial y_i} = 
\begin{cases}
    -\phi'(y_1) -\psi'(-y_1)\phi(-y_2) -\psi'(y_1)\phi(y_2), & i = 1, \\
    -\big(\psi(-y_{i-1})+\psi(y_{i-1})\big)\phi'(y_i) -\psi'(-y_i)\phi(-y_{i+1})-\psi'(y_i)\phi(y_{i+1}), & i=2,\dots,T-1, \\
    -\big(\psi(-y_{T-1})+\psi(y_{T-1})\big)\phi'(y_T), & i=T. \\
\end{cases}
\end{split}
\end{equation}

According to Lemma~\ref{lem:gate-properties}(b) and (c) and Lemma~\ref{lem:gate-paired-properties}, we have
\[
    0\le (\psi(-y_{i-1})+\psi(y_{i-1}))\phi'(y_i) \le1
~~~~~~\text{and}~~~~~~
    0\le
    \psi'(-y_i)\phi(-y_{i+1})
    +\psi'(y_i)\phi(y_{i+1})
    \le8.
\]
Combing with equation~(\ref{eq:hard-chain-gradient-coordinate}) implies
\begin{equation*}                                     
    \left\| \nabla\bar f_T({\bf{y}}) \right\| 
= \sqrt{T} \max_{i\in[T]}\left|\frac{\partial\bar f_T}{\partial y_i}\right|
\le9\sqrt T.
\end{equation*}
We now consider the bound of Hessian. 
Lemma~\ref{lem:gate-properties}(c) implies
\[
    \left|\frac{\partial^2 A_1({\bf{y}})}{\partial y_1^2}\right|
    =|\phi''(y_1)|\le2.
\]
For all $i\ge2$, Lemma~\ref{lem:gate-properties}(c) and \ref{lem:gate-paired-properties} imply

\begin{align}
& \left|\frac{\partial^2 A_i({\bf{y}})}{\partial y_{i-1}^2}\right|
= |\psi''(-y_{i-1})\phi(-y_i)     -\psi''(y_{i-1})\phi(y_i)|
\le2(|\psi''(-y_{i-1})|+|\psi''(y_{i-1})|)
\le48, \label{eq:hard-A-xx-bound} \\[0.15cm] 
& \left|\frac{\partial^2 A_i({\bf{y}})}{\partial y_i^2}\right|
= |-(\psi(-y_{i-1})+\psi(y_{i-1}))\phi''(y_i)| \le2, \label{eq:hard-A-zz-bound} \\[0.15cm]
& \left|\frac{\partial^2 A_i({\bf{y}})}{\partial y_{i-1}\partial y_i}\right|
 = |(\psi'(-y_{i-1})-\psi'(y_{i-1}))\phi'(y_i)|
\le4.    \label{eq:hard-A-xz-bound}
\end{align}
Note that each $A_i({\bf{y}})$ depends only on $y_{i-1}$ and $y_i$ for $i\ge2$, which implies the Hessian of $\bar f_T({\bf{y}})$ is tridiagonal matrix, i.e.,
\begin{equation*}
    \frac{\partial^2\bar f_T({\bf{y}})}{\partial y_i\partial y_j}=0
    ~~~\text{for all}~~~i,j\in[T]~~~\text{such that}~~~|i-j|\ge2.
\end{equation*}
According to equations (\ref{eq:hard-A-xx-bound}) and (\ref{eq:hard-A-zz-bound}), the absolute value of each diagonal entry of $\nabla^2\bar f_T({\bf{y}})$ is bounded by $48+2=50$. 
Moreover, equation~(\ref{eq:hard-A-xz-bound}) implies that each nonzero off-diagonal entry of $\nabla^2\bar f_T({\bf{y}})$ has absolute value at most $4$.
Hence, every row of $\nabla^2\bar f_T({\bf{y}})$ has absolute row sum at most $50+2\cdot4=58$. 
Since the Hessian is symmetric, its spectral norm is bounded by its maximum absolute row sum, which implies
\begin{equation}
    \left\| \nabla^2\bar f_T({\bf{y}}) \right\|
    \le\left\| \nabla^2\bar f_T({\bf{y}}) \right\|_\infty
    \le58     
    \label{eq:hard-chain-hessian-bound}
\end{equation}

\paragraph{The proof of statement (c).}
We let $i\in[T]$ be the smallest index such that $|y_i|\le1$. 
If $i=1$, then equation~(\ref{eq:hard-chain-gradient-coordinate}) and the nonnegativity of $\psi'$ and $\phi$ from Lemma~\ref{lem:gate-properties}(b) and (c) implies
\[
    \frac{\partial\bar f_T({\bf{y}})}{\partial y_1}
    \le-\phi'(y_1).
\]
Combining with $|y_1|\le1$ and Lemma~\ref{lem:gate-properties}(d), we achieve
\[
    \left|\frac{\partial\bar f_T({\bf{y}})}{\partial y_1}\right|
    \ge\phi'(y_1)>\frac25.
\]
If $i\ge2$, the definition of $i$ implies $|y_{i-1}|>1$. 
According to Lemma~\ref{lem:gate-properties}(a), we obtain
\begin{equation}
    \psi(-y_{i-1})+\psi(y_{i-1})=1.
    \label{eq:previous-gate-one}
\end{equation}
Substituting equation~(\ref{eq:previous-gate-one}) into equation~(\ref{eq:hard-chain-gradient-coordinate}) and using the non-negativity of $\psi'$ and $\phi$ from Lemma~\ref{lem:gate-properties}(b) and (c), we have
\[
    \frac{\partial\bar f_T({\bf{y}})}{\partial y_i}
    \le-\phi'(y_i).
\]
Since $|y_i|\le1$, Lemma~\ref{lem:gate-properties}(d) implies
\[
    \left|\frac{\partial\bar f_T({\bf{y}})}{\partial y_i}\right|
    \ge\phi'(y_i)>\frac25.
\]
Combing above two inequality, we obtain
\begin{equation}
    \left\| \nabla\bar f_T({\bf{y}}) \right\|
    \ge
    \left|\frac{\partial\bar f_T}{\partial y_i}\right|
    >
    \frac25.
    \label{eq:hard-chain-certificate}
\end{equation}


\paragraph{The proof of statement (d).}
We now establish the gradient-dependent upper bound for Hessian.
We first consider the case that there exists some $i\in[T]$ such that $|y_i|\le1$. 
By equation~(\ref{eq:hard-chain-hessian-bound}) and equation~(\ref{eq:hard-chain-certificate}), we obtain
\begin{equation}
    \left\| \nabla^2\bar f_T({\bf{y}}) \right\|
    \le 58
    \leq 160\cdot\frac25
    \le160\left\| \nabla\bar f_T({\bf{y}}) \right\|.
    \label{eq:hard-chain-curvature-case-one}
\end{equation}
We then consider the case that $|y_i|>1$ holds for all $i\in[T]$. 
According to Lemma~\ref{lem:gate-properties}(a), we have
\[
    \psi(-y_i)+\psi(y_i)=1.
\]
Moreover, since both $y_i$ and $-y_i$ do not lie in the interval $(1/2,1)$, equation~(\ref{eq:gate-pair-derivative-zero}) implies
\[
    \psi'(-y_i)=\psi'(y_i)=0.
\]
Substituting the above two identities into equation~(\ref{eq:hard-chain-gradient-coordinate}), we obtain
\begin{equation}
    \frac{\partial\bar f_T({\bf{y}})}{\partial y_i}
    =-\phi'(y_i)
    \quad \text{for all}~~i\in[T].
    \label{eq:hard-chain-saturated-gradient}
\end{equation}
Hence, the Hessian of $\bar f_T({\bf{y}})$ is diagonal and satisfies
\begin{equation*}
    \nabla^2\bar f_T({\bf{y}})=-\operatorname{diag}\big(\phi''(y_1),\ldots,\phi''(y_T)\big).
                                            
\end{equation*}
Consequently, Lemma~\ref{lem:gate-properties}(c) and equation~(\ref{eq:hard-chain-saturated-gradient}) imply
\begin{align}
    \left\| \nabla^2\bar f_T({\bf{y}}) \right\|=
    \max_{i\in[T]}|\phi''(y_i)|
    \le2\max_{i\in[T]}\phi'(y_i)
    \le2\left\| \nabla\bar f_T({\bf{y}}) \right\|
    \le160\left\| \nabla\bar f_T({\bf{y}}) \right\|.
    \label{eq:hard-chain-curvature-case-two}
\end{align}
Combining equations (\ref{eq:hard-chain-curvature-case-one}) and  (\ref{eq:hard-chain-curvature-case-two}), we conclude that
\begin{equation*}
    \left\| \nabla^2\bar f_T({\bf{y}}) \right\|
    \le160\left\| \nabla\bar f_T({\bf{y}}) \right\|
    \qquad
\end{equation*}
for all ${\bf{y}}\in{\mathbb{R}}^T$.



\paragraph{The proof of statement (e).}
Follow the notation defined in Section \ref{sec:Preliminaries}, we let
\begin{align*}
    \mathrm{prog}_{1/4}({\bf{y}}):=\max\{i\in{\mathbb{N}} : |y_i| > 1/4\}.
\end{align*}
for given ${\bf{y}}=[y_1, \dots, y_T]\in{\mathbb{R}}^T$.
For each $i>\operatorname{prog}_{1/4}({\bf{y}})+1$, we have 
\begin{align}\label{eq:y_i14}
|y_i| \le 1/4 \qquad\text{and}\qquad |y_{i-1}| \le 1/4.    
\end{align}
Combining Lemma~\ref{lem:gate-properties}(a) and equation equation~(\ref{eq:gate-pair-derivative-zero}), equation~(\ref{eq:y_i14}) implies
\[
    \psi(-y_{i-1})=\psi(y_{i-1})=0  \qquad\text{and}\qquad     \psi'(-y_i)=\psi'(y_i)=0.
\]
Substituting the above results into equation~(\ref{eq:hard-chain-gradient-coordinate}), we obtain
\[
    \frac{\partial\bar f_T({\bf{y}})}{\partial y_i}=0
\]
for all $i>\operatorname{prog}_{1/4}({\bf{y}})+1$.
Hence, it holds
\begin{equation*}
    \operatorname{prog}_0\big(\nabla\bar f_T({\bf{y}})\big)
    \le\operatorname{prog}_{1/4}({\bf{y}})+1.
\end{equation*}

label: eq:scaled-hessian-formula
title: Proof
body_md:
Recall that the definition of $f_{{\bf U}}({\bf{x}})=aH_{{\bf U},\mu}({\bf{x}}/b)$ in equation~(\ref{eq:scaled-hard-function}) implies 
\begin{align}
    \nabla f_{{\bf U}}({\bf{x}})
    =\frac{a}{b}\nabla H_{{\bf U},\mu}\left(\frac{{\bf{x}}}{b}\right),
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
    \nabla^2 f_{{\bf U}}({\bf{x}}) = \frac{a}{b^2}\nabla^2 H_{{\bf U},\mu}\left(\frac{{\bf{x}}}{b}\right).
    \label{eq:scaled-hessian-formula}
\end{align}
We verify the properties of the function $f_{{\bf U}}({\bf{x}})$ as follows.

\paragraph{The proof of statement (a).}
Combining the gradient-dependent curvature bound equation~(\ref{eq:global-hard-curvature}) and equation~(\ref{eq:scaled-hessian-formula}), we have
\begin{align}\label{eq:scaled-hessian-intermediate}
\begin{split}    
& \left\| \nabla^2 f_{{\bf U}}({\bf{x}}) \right\| 
= \frac{a}{b^2}\left\| \nabla^2 H_{{\bf U},\mu}\left(\frac{{\bf{x}}}{b}\right) \right\| \\
\leq &  \frac{240a}{b^2}\left(
    \left\| \nabla H_{{\bf U},\mu}({\bf{x}}) \right\|
    +\mu\log\frac1\mu
    \right) \\
=&  \frac{240}{b}\left\| \nabla f_{{\bf U}}({\bf{x}}) \right\|
    +\frac{240a\mu}{b^2}\log\frac1\mu \\
=& \frac{L_1}{2}\left\| \nabla f_{{\bf U}}({\bf{x}}) \right\|
    +8L_1\epsilon\mu\log\frac1\mu,
\end{split}
\end{align}
where the last step follows from the setting $b=480/L_1$ and $a/b=16\epsilon$ in equation~(\ref{eq:hard-scaling-parameters}).
For the term $\mu\log(1/\mu)$, recall we set
\begin{align}
    \delta_0=\min\left\{10^{-2},\frac{L_0}{16L_1\epsilon}\right\}\in(0, 10^{-2}]
    \qquad \text{and} \qquad
    \mu=\frac{\delta_0}{4\log(\mathrm e/\delta_0)}
    \label{eq:hard-scaling-parameters1}
\end{align}
in equation~(\ref{eq:hard-scaling-parameters}), which implies
\begin{align*}
    \log\frac1\mu
    =
    \log\frac1{\delta_0}
    +\log\left(4\log\frac{\mathrm e}{\delta_0}\right)
    \le 2\log\frac1{\delta_0}+\log4 <2\log\frac{\mathrm e}{\delta_0},
                             
\end{align*}
where the first inequality uses $\log t\le t-1$ for all $t>0$. 
Combining with the definition of $\delta_0$ and $\mu$ in equation~(\ref{eq:hard-scaling-parameters1}), it holds
\begin{equation}
    \mu\log\frac1\mu
    \le\frac{\delta_0}{2}
    \le\frac{L_0}{32L_1\epsilon}.
    \label{eq:scaled-mu-bound}
\end{equation} 

Combining equation~(\ref{eq:scaled-hessian-intermediate}) and
equation~(\ref{eq:scaled-mu-bound}), we know that for all ${\bf{x}}\in{\mathbb{R}}^d$, it holds
\begin{align*}
    \left\| \nabla^2 f_{{\bf U}}({\bf{x}}) \right\|
    &\le
    \frac{L_1}{2}\left\| \nabla f_{{\bf U}}({\bf{x}}) \right\|
    +8L_1\epsilon\mu\log\frac1\mu
    \\
    &\le
    \frac{L_1}{2}\left\| \nabla f_{{\bf U}}({\bf{x}}) \right\|
    +4L_1\epsilon\delta_0
    \\
    &\le
    \frac12\left(
    L_0+L_1\left\| \nabla f_{{\bf U}}({\bf{x}}) \right\|
    \right).
\end{align*}
Following Corollary A.4 of \citet{zhang2020improved} by replacing their parameters $L_0$, $L_1$, and $c$ with~$L_0/2$, $L_1/2$, and $1$, respectively, we obtain
\begin{align*}   
    \left\| \nabla f_{{\bf U}}({\bf{y}})-\nabla f_{{\bf U}}({\bf{x}}) \right\|
    &\le
    \left(
    L_0+\frac{(\mathrm e-1)L_1
    \left\| \nabla f_{{\bf U}}({\bf{x}}) \right\|}{2}
    \right)\left\| {\bf{y}}-{\bf{x}} \right\| \\
    &\le
    \left(
    L_0+L_1\left\| \nabla f_{{\bf U}}({\bf{x}}) \right\|
    \right)\left\| {\bf{y}}-{\bf{x}} \right\|,
\end{align*}
for all ${\bf{x}},{\bf{y}}\in{\mathbb{R}}^d$ with $\left\| {\bf{y}}-{\bf{x}} \right\|\le 1/L_1\le 2/L_1$.
Thus, the function $f_{{\bf U}}$ is $(L_0,L_1)$-smooth.

\paragraph{The proof of statement (b).}
Since $a,b>0$, the definition of the function $f_{{\bf U}}$ in equation~(\ref{eq:scaled-hard-function}) and the initial optimality gap bound equation~(\ref{eq:global-hard-gap}) imply
\begin{align*}
    f_{{\bf U}}({\bf{0}})
    -\inf_{{\bf{x}}\in{\mathbb{R}}^d}f_{{\bf U}}({\bf{x}})
    &=
    a\left(
    H_{{\bf U},\mu}({\bf{0}})
    -\inf_{{\bf{x}}\in{\mathbb{R}}^d}H_{{\bf U},\mu}\left(\frac{{\bf{x}}}{b}\right)
    \right) \\
    &=
    a\left(
    H_{{\bf U},\mu}({\bf{0}})
    -\inf_{{\bf{x}}\in{\mathbb{R}}^d}H_{{\bf U},\mu}({\bf{x}})
    \right)
    \le2aT,
                                  
\end{align*}
where the second equality follows from the fact that the mapping ${\bf{x}}\mapsto{\bf{x}}/b$ is a bijection on ${\mathbb{R}}^d$.

\paragraph{The proof of statement (c).}
Let $i$ be the index $i\in[T]$ such that
\[
    \left|
    \left[
    {\bf U}^\top\rho_R\left(\frac{{\bf{x}}}{b}\right)
    \right]_i
    \right|\le1.
\]
By the gradient formula in equation~(\ref{eq:scaled-hessian-formula}) and equation~(\ref{eq:global-hard-gradient}), we obtain
\begin{equation*}
    \left\| \nabla f_{{\bf U}}({\bf{x}}) \right\|
    =
    \frac{a}{b}
    \left\| \nabla H_{{\bf U},\mu}\left(\frac{{\bf{x}}}{b}\right) \right\|
    \ge
    \frac{a}{4b}
    =
    4\epsilon,
                                           
\end{equation*}
where the last equality follows from the setting $a/b=16\epsilon$ in equation~(\ref{eq:hard-scaling-parameters}).

body_md:
\label{lem:mask-one-step}
For given ${\bf{y}}=[y_1,\dots,y_T]\in{\mathbb{R}}^T$,
suppose there exists some $s\in\{0,\ldots,T-1\}$ such that
$|y_{s+1}|,\ldots,|y_T|\le1/4$.
Then the stochastic component $\bar F_T$ defined in equation~(\ref{eq:stochastic-chain}) satisfies:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*),leftmargin=0.65cm]
    \item If $Z=0$, then
    $\operatorname{supp}(\nabla\bar F_T({\bf{y}};0))
    \subseteq[s]$ and
    $\nabla\bar F_T({\bf{y}};0)
    =\nabla\bar F_T(\Pi_s({\bf{y}});0)$.

    \item If $Z=1$, then
    $\operatorname{supp}(\nabla\bar F_T({\bf{y}};1))
    \subseteq[s+1]$ and
    $\nabla\bar F_T({\bf{y}};1)
    =\nabla\bar F_T(\Pi_{s+1}({\bf{y}});1)$.
\end{enumerate}
Here, we denote  $\Pi_s({\bf{y}})=[y_1,\dots,y_s,0,\dots,0]^\top$.

title: Proof
body_md:
The verify properties of functions $\bar F_T$ and $Q_T$.

\paragraph{The proof of statement (a).}
According to equation~(\ref{eq:masking-Q-decomposition}) and the product rule, we know that
\begin{equation}
    \nabla Q_T({\bf{y}})
    =
    \sum_{i=1}^{T}
    \left(
    \Theta_i({\bf{y}})\nabla A_i({\bf{y}})
    +A_i({\bf{y}})\nabla\Theta_i({\bf{y}})
    \right).
    \label{eq:grad-Bi}
\end{equation}
We denote
\begin{equation*}
    m:=\operatorname{prog}_{1/2}({\bf{y}})
    \in\{0,1,\ldots,T\}.
\end{equation*}
For any $m\in\{0,1,\ldots,T\}$ and $i\ge m+2$, we have $|y_{i-1}|\le1/2$. Hence, Lemma~\ref{lem:gate-properties}(a) and equation~(\ref{eq:gate-pair-derivative-zero}) implies
\[
    \psi(y_{i-1}) = \psi(-y_{i-1})
    =\psi'(y_{i-1})=\psi'(-y_{i-1})=0.
\]
Combing above results with equation~(\ref{eq:hard-zero-chain}) gives
$A_i({\bf{y}})=0$ and $\nabla A_i({\bf{y}})={\bf{0}}$, which implies
\begin{equation}
     \Theta_i({\bf{y}})\nabla A_i({\bf{y}})+A_i({\bf{y}})\nabla\Theta_i({\bf{y}})={\bf{0}}
    ~~~~~\text{for all}~i\ge m+2.
    \label{eq:Bi-right-zero}
\end{equation}

In the case of $m=0$, combing equations (\ref{eq:grad-Bi}) and (\ref{eq:Bi-right-zero}) implies
\begin{align}\label{eq:Bi-left-zero-0}
    \nabla Q_T({\bf{y}})
    = \Theta_1({\bf{y}})\nabla A_1({\bf{y}})+A_1({\bf{y}})\nabla\Theta_1({\bf{y}})  
\end{align}
In the case of $m\in[T]$, we have $|y_m|>1/2$. Hence, equation~(\ref{eq:chi-flat-values}) and equation~(\ref{eq:chi-flat-values2}) imply
\[
    \chi(y_m)=\chi'(y_m)=0.
\]
Note that for all $i\le m$, equations~(\ref{eq:masking-functions}) and (\ref{eq:theta-coordinate-derivative}) yield
\[
    \Theta_i({\bf{y}})=\prod_{k=i}^{T}\chi(y_k)=0
    \qquad\text{and}\qquad
    \nabla\Theta_i({\bf{y}})={\bf{0}},
\]
respectively. This implies
\begin{equation}
    \Theta_i({\bf{y}})\nabla A_i({\bf{y}})+A_i({\bf{y}})\nabla\Theta_i({\bf{y}})={\bf{0}}
    ~~~~~\text{for all}~i\le m.
    \label{eq:Bi-left-zero}
\end{equation}
Combining equations (\ref{eq:Bi-right-zero}), (\ref{eq:Bi-left-zero-0}) and (\ref{eq:Bi-left-zero}), we obtain
\begin{equation}
    \nabla Q_T({\bf{y}})=
    \begin{cases}
        \Theta_{m+1}({\bf{y}})\nabla A_{m+1}({\bf{y}})+A_{m+1}({\bf{y}})\nabla\Theta_{m+1}({\bf{y}})
        & \text{if}~m<T,\\[0.1cm]
        {\bf{0}}, & \text{if}~m=T.
    \end{cases}
    \label{eq:single-active-B}
\end{equation}

We now establish the upper bound on $\left\| \nabla Q_T({\bf{y}}) \right\|$ by considering the following three cases.
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=0.65cm]
\item In the case of $m=0$, we have $A_1({\bf{y}})=-\phi(y_1)$, so that Lemma~\ref{lem:gate-properties}(c) implies
$|A_1({\bf{y}})|<2$ and~$\left\| \nabla A_1({\bf{y}}) \right\|\le1$.
By equation~(\ref{eq:single-active-B}), equation~(\ref{eq:chi-range}), and Lemma~\ref{lem:theta-gradient}, we obtain
\begin{align*}
    \left\| \nabla Q_T({\bf{y}}) \right\|
    &\le
    |\Theta_1({\bf{y}})|\left\| \nabla A_1({\bf{y}}) \right\|+|A_1({\bf{y}})|\left\| \nabla\Theta_1({\bf{y}}) \right\|
    \\
    &\le1+2\cdot120
    =241<249.
\end{align*}

\item In the case of $m\in[T-1]$, combining the definition of $A_i({\bf{y}})$ in equation~(\ref{eq:hard-zero-chain}) with equation~(\ref{eq:gate-pair-value}) and Lemma~\ref{lem:gate-properties}(c) imply
\begin{equation}
    |A_{m+1}({\bf{y}})|
    = |\psi(-y_{m})\phi(-y_{m+1})-\psi(y_{m})\phi(y_{m+1})|
    \le 2(\psi(-y_m)+\psi(y_m))
    \le 2.
    \label{eq:Aj-bound}
\end{equation}
Moreover, combining the definition of $A_i({\bf{y}})$ in equation~(\ref{eq:hard-zero-chain}) with equation~(\ref{eq:gate-pair-first}), equation~(\ref{eq:gate-pair-value}), and Lemma~\ref{lem:gate-properties}(c), we have
\begin{align*}
    &\left|\frac{\partial A_{m+1}({\bf{y}})}{\partial y_m}\right|
    = |\psi'(-y_{m})\phi(-y_{m+1})+\psi'(y_{m})\phi(y_{m+1})|
    \le
    2|\psi'(-y_m)+\psi'(y_m)|
    \le8,\\
    &\left|\frac{\partial A_{m+1}({\bf{y}})}{\partial y_{m+1}}\right|
    = |\psi(-y_{m})\phi'(-y_{m+1})+\psi(y_{m})\phi'(y_{m+1})|
    \leq |\psi(-y_m)+\psi(y_m)|
    \le1,
\end{align*}
Since the function $A_{m+1}({\bf{y}})$ depends only on $y_m$ and $y_{m+1}$, the above results leads to
\begin{equation}
    \left\| \nabla A_{m+1}({\bf{y}}) \right\|
    \le\sqrt{8^2+1^2}
    =\sqrt{65}<9.
    \label{eq:grad-Aj-bound}
\end{equation}
Therefore, combining equation~(\ref{eq:single-active-B}) with equations (\ref{eq:masking-functions}), (\ref{eq:chi-range}), (\ref{eq:grad-Aj-bound}), and (\ref{eq:Aj-bound}), and Lemma~\ref{lem:theta-gradient}, we have
\begin{align}
\begin{split}    
    \left\| \nabla Q_T({\bf{y}}) \right\|
    &\le
    |\Theta_{m+1}({\bf{y}})|
    \left\| \nabla A_{m+1}({\bf{y}}) \right\|
    +|A_{m+1}({\bf{y}})|
    \left\| \nabla\Theta_{m+1}({\bf{y}}) \right\| \\
    &\le9+2\cdot120
    =249.
    \label{eq:Q-gradient-bound}
\end{split}
\end{align}

\item 
In the case of $m=T$, equation~(\ref{eq:single-active-B}) directly gives 
$\left\| \nabla Q_T({\bf{y}}) \right\|=0\le249$.
\end{enumerate}
Therefore, the above derivations conclude $\left\| \nabla Q_T({\bf{y}}) \right\|\le249$ holds for all ${\bf{y}}\in{\mathbb{R}}^T$.

\paragraph{The proof of statement (b).}
Differentiating equation~(\ref{eq:stochastic-chain}) obtains
\begin{equation*}
    {\bf{g}}_T({\bf{y}};Z)
    =
    \nabla\bar f_T({\bf{y}})
    +
    \left(\frac Zq-1\right)\nabla Q_T({\bf{y}}).
\end{equation*}
The distribution $Z\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(q)$ indicates ${\mathbb{E}}_Z[Z/q-1]=0$, resulting
\begin{equation*}
    {\mathbb{E}}_Z[{\bf{g}}_T({\bf{y}};Z)]
    =
    \nabla\bar f_T({\bf{y}}).
\end{equation*}

We then verify the property of probability-$q$ zero-chain for ${\bf{g}}_T({\bf{y}};Z)$. Fix given ${\bf{y}}\in{\mathbb{R}}^T$, we let 
\begin{align*}
s=\operatorname{prog}_{1/4}({\bf{y}}).     
\end{align*}
We show that ${\bf{g}}_T({\bf{y}};Z)$ is $q$-probability zero-chain by verifying conditions (\ref{eq:prob-zero-chain-no-progress}) and
(\ref{eq:prob-zero-chain-one-progress}) as follows.
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=0.65cm]
\item If $s<T$, the definition of $s$ implies $|y_{s+1}|,\ldots,|y_T|\le1/4$. Hence, when $Z=0$, we can apply Lemma~\ref{lem:mask-one-step}(a) to achieve
\begin{align}\label{eq:p-zero-chain-0}    
    \operatorname{prog}_0({\bf{g}}_T({\bf{y}};0))
    \le s
    \quad\text{and}\quad
    {\bf{g}}_T({\bf{y}};0)
    =
    {\bf{g}}_T(\Pi_s({\bf{y}});0)
    \quad \text{for all } {\bf{y}}\in{\mathbb{R}}^T.
\end{align}
Recall that $\mathbb P(Z=0)=1-q$, then equation~(\ref{eq:p-zero-chain-0}) verifies that condition equation~(\ref{eq:prob-zero-chain-no-progress})  with~$\theta=q$.
When $Z=1$, wen can apply Lemma~\ref{lem:mask-one-step}(b) to achieve
\begin{align}\label{eq:p-zero-chain-1}
    \operatorname{prog}_0({\bf{g}}_T({\bf{y}};1))
    \le s+1 
    \quad\text{and}\quad
    {\bf{g}}_T({\bf{y}};1) =
    {\bf{g}}_T(\Pi_{s+1}({\bf{y}});1)
    \quad \text{for all } {\bf{y}}\in{\mathbb{R}}^T.
\end{align}
According to Lemma~\ref{lem:mask-one-step}(a), we know that equation~(\ref{eq:p-zero-chain-1}) also holds when $Z=0$.
Hence, we have verifies condition (\ref{eq:prob-zero-chain-one-progress})  with $\theta=q$.

\item If $s=T$, we have $\operatorname{prog}_{1/4}({\bf{y}})=T$ and $\Pi_{1+\operatorname{prog}_{1/4}}({\bf{y}})=\Pi_{1+\operatorname{prog}_{1/4}}({\bf{y}})={\bf{y}}$. Therefore, for all ${\bf{y}}\in{\mathbb{R}}^T$, all conditions
\begin{align*}    
   \operatorname{prog}_0({\bf{g}}_T({\bf{y}};Z))
    \le \operatorname{prog}_{1/4}({\bf{y}}),\quad
    {\bf{g}}_T({\bf{y}};Z)
    = {\bf{g}}_T\bigl(
    \Pi_{\operatorname{prog}_{1/4}({\bf{y}})}({\bf{y}});Z
    \bigr), \\
    \operatorname{prog}_0({\bf{g}}_T({\bf{y}};Z))
    \le1+\operatorname{prog}_{1/4}({\bf{y}}),\quad
    {\bf{g}}_T({\bf{y}};Z)
    = {\bf{g}}_T\bigl(
    \Pi_{1+\operatorname{prog}_{1/4}({\bf{y}})}({\bf{y}});Z
    \bigr)
\end{align*}
holds in both cases of $Z=0$ and $Z=1$.
This verifies equations (\ref{eq:prob-zero-chain-no-progress}) and (\ref{eq:prob-zero-chain-one-progress}).
\end{enumerate}
Hence, we conclude that ${\bf{g}}_T$ is a probability-$q$ zero-chain.

body_md:
According to Lemma~\ref{lem:information-hiding}, we know that 
the gradient evaluation ${\bf{g}}_T({\bf{y}};Z)$ is a probability-$q$ zero-chain.
Moreover, the definition of $\rho$ implies $\left\| \rho_R({\bf{x}}/b) \right\|\le R$ for every ${\bf{x}}\in{\mathbb{R}}^d$.
Note that the proof of Lemma 5 of \citet{arjevani2023lower} only require the oracle is a probability zero-chain, so that we can use this lemma with $K=1$ to achieve 
\[
    \operatorname{prog}_{{1}/{4}}\big({\bf U}^{\top}\rho_{R}({\bf{x}}_{\mathsf{A}}^{(t)}/b) \big)< T
\]
for all $t\le(T-\log(2/\delta))/(2q)$.
Hence, we have
\[
    \left|
    [{\bf U}^\top\rho_R({\bf{x}}^{(t)}/b)]_T
    \right|
    \le\frac14.
\]

According to Lemma~\ref{lem:global-hard-properties},
we obtain
\[
    \left\| \nabla H_{{\bf U},\mu}({\bf{x}}^{(t)}/b) \right\|
    \ge\frac14.
\]
Based on the definition  
\[
    \nabla f_{{\bf U}}({\bf{x}})
    =
    \frac ab\nabla H_{{\bf U},\mu}({\bf{x}}/b),
\]
with $a/b=16\epsilon$, it follows that
\[
    \left\| \nabla f_{{\bf U}}({\bf{x}}^{(t)}) \right\|
    \ge4\epsilon.
\]
This completes the proof.

If ${\bf{g}}={\bf{0}}$ and $\gamma=0$, the result is trivial. Hence, we focus on the case of $\|{\bf{g}}\|+\gamma>0$.
According to Cauchy–Schwarz inequality and triangle inequality, we achieve 
\[
\begin{aligned}
\langle {\bf{h}},\varphi_\gamma({\bf{g}})\rangle
&=\frac{\|{\bf{g}}\|^2+\langle {\bf{h}}-{\bf{g}},{\bf{g}}\rangle}{\|{\bf{g}}\|+\gamma}\\
&\ge \frac{\|{\bf{g}}\|^2}{\|{\bf{g}}\|+\gamma}
      -\frac{\|{\bf{h}}-{\bf{g}}\|\cdot\|{\bf{g}}\|}{\|{\bf{g}}\|+\gamma}\\
&\ge \|{\bf{g}}\|-\gamma-\|{\bf{h}}-{\bf{g}}\|\\
&\ge \|{\bf{h}}\|-\gamma-2\|{\bf{h}}-{\bf{g}}\|.
\end{aligned}
\]
This finishes the proof.
